stem: The most important and universal international organisation, established after the Second World War to maintain peace and promote cooperation, is the __________.
solution: The UNITED NATIONS (UN) is the most important and universal international organisation, established in 1945 after the SECOND WORLD WAR to maintain international PEACE and SECURITY and to promote COOPERATION among nations (in economic, social, humanitarian, and other fields). Nearly all the world's states are members. It replaced the earlier, failed League of Nations. So the key post-war international organisation is the UN. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The United Nations was established in __________.
solution: The United Nations was established in 1945, in the aftermath of the SECOND WORLD WAR (its Charter came into force in October 1945). It was created to prevent another such catastrophic war, to maintain international peace and security, and to foster cooperation among nations. (The League of Nations, its predecessor, was set up in 1919/1920 after the First World War but failed to prevent the Second.) So the UN was established in 1945. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The UN succeeded an earlier international organisation that had failed to prevent the Second World War, called the __________.
solution: The UN succeeded the LEAGUE of NATIONS — the earlier international organisation founded after the First World War (1919/1920) to preserve peace. The League FAILED to prevent aggression and the outbreak of the Second World War (weakened by the absence of major powers like the USA, and by its inability to enforce its decisions). Learning from the League's failures, the victors of WWII created the stronger UN in 1945. So the UN's failed predecessor was the League of Nations. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The main organs of the United Nations include the General Assembly, the Security Council, and __________.
options: The Secretariat, the International Court of Justice, and the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)
The IMF and World Bank only
solution: The main organs of the United Nations include: the GENERAL ASSEMBLY (all members, one vote each); the SECURITY COUNCIL (responsible for peace and security); the SECRETARIAT (the UN's administrative body, headed by the Secretary-General); the INTERNATIONAL COURT of JUSTICE (ICJ, the UN's judicial organ, at The Hague); the ECONOMIC and SOCIAL COUNCIL (ECOSOC); and (historically) the Trusteeship Council. So the main organs include the Secretariat, the ICJ, and ECOSOC (alongside the Assembly and Security Council). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The UN organ with the primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security is the __________.
solution: The UN organ with the PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY for maintaining international PEACE and SECURITY is the SECURITY COUNCIL. It can take binding decisions and strong measures — including authorising sanctions, peacekeeping operations, and even the use of force — to address threats to peace, breaches of the peace, and acts of aggression. Its decisions are binding on all UN members. So the peace-and-security organ is the Security Council. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The UN Security Council has __________ permanent members with veto power.
options: Five (the USA, Russia, the UK, France, and China)
solution: The UN Security Council has FIVE PERMANENT members (the 'P5') with VETO power: the UNITED STATES, RUSSIA (which took the USSR's seat), the UNITED KINGDOM, FRANCE, and CHINA. These were the principal victors of the Second World War. In addition, the Council has ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms (making 15 members in total). The five permanent members can VETO (block) any substantive resolution. So the Security Council has five veto-wielding permanent members. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The 'veto' power held by the five permanent members of the Security Council means that __________.
options: Any one of them can single-handedly block (defeat) a substantive Security Council resolution, even if all other members support it
They must all agree for the Council to meet
They can be voted out by the General Assembly
solution: The 'VETO' power held by the five permanent members (P5) means that ANY ONE of them can SINGLE-HANDEDLY BLOCK (defeat) a SUBSTANTIVE Security Council resolution — a negative vote by even one permanent member prevents the resolution from passing, EVEN if all the other 14 members support it. This gives the P5 enormous, disproportionate power over the Council's decisions (and is a major point of criticism, as it can paralyse the Council when a great power's interests are involved). So the veto lets any one P5 member block a resolution. This is a prelims-critical concept.

stem: The UN General Assembly is distinctive because __________.
options: All member states are represented and each has ONE equal vote (it is the main deliberative body, a kind of 'world parliament', though its resolutions are generally non-binding recommendations)
It has the power to declare war on any country
Its decisions are always legally binding on all
solution: The UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY is distinctive because ALL MEMBER STATES are represented in it, and each has ONE EQUAL VOTE (regardless of size or power) — making it a kind of 'world parliament' and the main DELIBERATIVE body of the UN, where global issues are debated and the collective voice of the world community (including small and poor nations) is expressed. However, its resolutions are generally RECOMMENDATIONS (non-binding), unlike the binding decisions of the Security Council. So the General Assembly features universal membership with one vote each, but mostly non-binding resolutions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The head of the UN Secretariat, the chief administrative officer of the UN, is the __________.
solution: The head of the UN SECRETARIAT — the chief administrative officer of the United Nations — is the SECRETARY-GENERAL. The Secretary-General manages the day-to-day work of the UN, oversees its agencies and staff, and plays an important diplomatic and moral role in international affairs (raising issues, mediating disputes, and representing the UN). The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council. So the UN's chief administrative officer is the Secretary-General. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: A major demand for the REFORM of the UN concerns the __________.
options: Security Council — its composition and the veto power are seen as outdated (reflecting the 1945 balance), and there are demands to expand permanent membership to include countries like India, and to make it more representative
solution: A major demand for the REFORM of the UN concerns the SECURITY COUNCIL. Its composition and the VETO power of the P5 are widely seen as OUTDATED — reflecting the power balance of 1945 (the WWII victors) rather than today's world. Critics argue the Council is UNREPRESENTATIVE (e.g., no permanent members from Africa, Latin America, or most of Asia; and rising powers excluded). There are strong demands to EXPAND the permanent membership to include major countries such as INDIA (and Japan, Germany, Brazil, and African representation), and to make the Council more representative, democratic, and effective. So the key reform demand concerns the Security Council's composition and veto. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India has been a strong candidate for permanent membership of a reformed UN Security Council. Which of the following supports India's claim?
options: India's large population, growing economy, democratic credentials, contributions to UN peacekeeping, and its role as a major responsible power
India's refusal to participate in the UN
India's lack of any global role
solution: India has been a strong candidate for PERMANENT MEMBERSHIP of a reformed UN Security Council. Its claim is supported by several factors: India's very LARGE POPULATION (about a sixth of humanity); its large and GROWING ECONOMY (a major world economy); its strong DEMOCRATIC credentials (the world's largest democracy); its substantial and long-standing CONTRIBUTIONS to UN PEACEKEEPING operations (one of the largest troop contributors); and its role as a major, responsible power committed to multilateralism. These factors make a compelling case that India deserves a permanent seat on a reformed Council. So option 1 lists the supports for India's claim. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Besides maintaining peace, the UN works through many specialised agencies. Which of the following is a UN specialised agency?
options: The WHO (World Health Organisation), UNESCO, UNICEF, ILO, and the FAO
solution: The UN works through many SPECIALISED AGENCIES and programmes that address specific global issues. Examples include: the WHO (World Health Organisation, for health); UNESCO (UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, for education, science, and culture); UNICEF (UN Children's Fund, for children's welfare); the ILO (International Labour Organisation, for labour rights); and the FAO (Food and Agriculture Organisation, for food and agriculture) — among others. These agencies carry out much of the UN's practical work in development and human welfare. So WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF, ILO, and FAO are UN agencies. (NATO, the Warsaw Pact, and ASEAN are NOT UN agencies.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank are important international economic institutions. The IMF's main role is to __________.
options: Oversee the international monetary/financial system and provide financial assistance/loans to countries facing balance-of-payments (economic) crises
solution: The INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND (IMF) is a key international economic institution whose main role is to OVERSEE the international MONETARY and FINANCIAL system, promote monetary cooperation and exchange-rate stability, and provide FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE/LOANS to member countries facing BALANCE-of-PAYMENTS or broader economic CRISES (often with policy conditions attached). It helps countries stabilise their economies. (The World Bank, by contrast, focuses on longer-term development lending.) So the IMF oversees the monetary system and lends to countries in crisis. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The World Bank's primary role is to __________.
options: Provide loans and assistance for long-term development projects (like infrastructure, poverty reduction, education, and health) in developing countries
solution: The WORLD BANK's primary role is to provide LOANS, grants, and technical ASSISTANCE for LONG-TERM DEVELOPMENT projects and programmes in developing countries — financing INFRASTRUCTURE (roads, dams, power), POVERTY REDUCTION, EDUCATION, HEALTH, and other development goals, with the broad aim of reducing poverty and promoting economic development. (This contrasts with the IMF's focus on short-term financial stability and balance-of-payments support.) So the World Bank funds long-term development in developing countries. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The organisation that deals with the rules of international trade among nations (promoting free trade and settling trade disputes) is the __________.
solution: The WORLD TRADE ORGANISATION (WTO) is the international body that deals with the RULES of INTERNATIONAL TRADE among nations. It works to promote FREE TRADE (by reducing tariffs and trade barriers through negotiated agreements), administers trade rules, and provides a mechanism for SETTLING TRADE DISPUTES between member countries. (It succeeded the earlier GATT in 1995.) So the international trade body is the WTO. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The IMF and World Bank are often criticised by developing countries because __________.
options: Their decision-making (voting power) is dominated by the rich Western countries (especially the USA), and the policy conditions they attach to loans can be harsh and unsuitable for developing economies
They give away too much free money
They are controlled by developing countries
They have no influence on economic policy
solution: The IMF and World Bank are often CRITICISED by developing countries on two main grounds. First, their DECISION-MAKING is weighted by financial contributions (a quota/share-based VOTING system), so it is DOMINATED by the rich WESTERN countries — especially the USA (which has effective veto power over major decisions) — while developing countries have a much smaller say. Second, the POLICY CONDITIONS (conditionalities) attached to their loans (such as structural adjustment — austerity, privatisation, deregulation, cuts in subsidies) can be HARSH, and are seen as often UNSUITABLE or damaging for developing economies and their poor. So these institutions are criticised for Western dominance and harsh loan conditions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: International organisations are important in world politics because they __________.
options: Help states cooperate, resolve disputes peacefully, provide a forum for dialogue, coordinate action on common problems, and establish rules/norms — even though they cannot force sovereign states to obey
Rule the world as a single government
Have their own armies to conquer countries
solution: International organisations are IMPORTANT in world politics because they help states COOPERATE and manage their interactions: they enable states to RESOLVE DISPUTES PEACEFULLY, provide a FORUM for DIALOGUE and negotiation, COORDINATE collective ACTION on COMMON PROBLEMS (like health, environment, poverty, and security), and establish RULES and NORMS of behaviour. However, they are NOT world governments — they generally CANNOT FORCE sovereign states to obey against their will (they rely on members' consent and cooperation). So international organisations facilitate cooperation and rule-making, without being able to compel states. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key limitation of the UN (and international organisations generally) is that __________.
options: It depends on the cooperation and will of its member states (especially the powerful ones), and it cannot compel a sovereign state — particularly a great power protected by the veto — to comply
It has unlimited power over all countries
It can conquer any country it wishes
solution: A KEY LIMITATION of the UN (and of international organisations in general) is that it DEPENDS on the COOPERATION and WILL of its member states — especially the POWERFUL ones — for its effectiveness and resources. It CANNOT COMPEL a sovereign state to comply with its wishes against that state's will; and it is particularly hamstrung when a GREAT POWER is involved, since the P5's VETO can BLOCK any strong Security Council action against themselves or their allies. This dependence on states and the veto can paralyse the UN and prevent it from acting decisively. So the UN's key limitation is its dependence on states and the constraint of the veto. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Despite its limitations, the UN has made important contributions, such as __________.
options: Peacekeeping operations, promotion of human rights, humanitarian and development work, and providing a forum where all nations (large and small) can be heard
solution: Despite its limitations, the UN has made many IMPORTANT CONTRIBUTIONS: it has conducted PEACEKEEPING operations to prevent or contain conflicts and help maintain ceasefires; it has promoted HUMAN RIGHTS (e.g., the Universal Declaration of Human Rights) and international law; it carries out vast HUMANITARIAN and DEVELOPMENT work (through agencies like WHO, UNICEF, UNHCR, and development programmes) helping the poor, refugees, children, and disaster victims; and it provides a vital FORUM where ALL nations — large and small — can be HEARD and can address global problems together. So the UN has contributed through peacekeeping, human rights, humanitarian/development work, and global dialogue. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The five permanent members dominate the UN Security Council. Reason (R): Their veto power allows any one of them to block substantive decisions, giving them disproportionate control over the Council. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the five PERMANENT members (P5) DOMINATE the UN Security Council. And the reason is (R) that their VETO POWER allows ANY ONE of them to BLOCK any substantive decision — even against the majority — giving the P5 DISPROPORTIONATE CONTROL over what the Council can and cannot do. This veto-based blocking power is precisely the mechanism through which the P5 dominate the Council (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): There are demands to reform the UN Security Council. Reason (R): Its current structure reflects the power realities of 1945 rather than those of today, and it excludes many important regions and rising powers (like India). Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that there are strong DEMANDS to REFORM the UN Security Council. And the reason is (R) that its CURRENT STRUCTURE (the P5 with vetoes) reflects the power realities of 1945 — the WWII victors — rather than TODAY's world, and it EXCLUDES many important REGIONS (Africa, Latin America) and RISING POWERS (like INDIA, Japan, Germany, Brazil), making it unrepresentative and, to many, undemocratic and outdated. This mismatch between the Council's structure and contemporary realities directly drives the demands for reform (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Besides states, other important actors in international organisations and world politics include __________.
options: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs), multinational corporations (MNCs), and international bodies — which also influence global affairs
solution: Besides STATES, other important ACTORS in international organisations and world politics include: NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATIONS (NGOs) — such as Amnesty International, the Red Cross, and Greenpeace — which advocate on issues like human rights, humanitarian relief, and the environment; MULTINATIONAL CORPORATIONS (MNCs), whose economic power spans borders; and various INTERNATIONAL BODIES and agencies. These non-state actors increasingly INFLUENCE global affairs — shaping agendas, providing services, and pressuring governments — alongside sovereign states. So NGOs, MNCs, and international bodies are important non-state actors. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is an international body concerned with __________.
options: Promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and preventing its diversion to nuclear weapons (nuclear safeguards and non-proliferation)
solution: The INTERNATIONAL ATOMIC ENERGY AGENCY (IAEA) is an international body (associated with the UN) concerned with NUCLEAR matters. Its main roles are to PROMOTE the PEACEFUL use of NUCLEAR ENERGY (for power, medicine, agriculture, etc.) and to PREVENT its DIVERSION to nuclear WEAPONS — through a system of SAFEGUARDS and inspections that verify countries are not misusing nuclear materials, thereby supporting nuclear NON-PROLIFERATION. So the IAEA deals with peaceful nuclear use and non-proliferation. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are examples of international __________.
options: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) that campaign for human rights
solution: AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL and HUMAN RIGHTS WATCH are examples of international NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATIONS (NGOs) that CAMPAIGN for HUMAN RIGHTS. They investigate and report on human-rights abuses around the world, advocate for the protection of rights, mobilise public opinion, and pressure governments and international bodies to act. As influential non-state actors, such NGOs play an important role in promoting human rights and holding states accountable. So they are human-rights NGOs. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'International Organisations' is that:
options: International organisations are useless and should be abolished

International organisations — above all the United Nations (with its main organs: the General Assembly, the veto-wielding Security Council, the Secretariat, the ICJ, and specialised agencies like WHO, UNICEF, and UNESCO) and economic bodies (the IMF, World Bank, and WTO) — play a vital role in helping sovereign states cooperate, maintain peace, resolve disputes, promote development and human rights, and address common global problems; yet they have important limitations (they depend on states' cooperation and cannot compel great powers, and bodies like the Security Council and the IMF/World Bank are seen as unrepresentative and dominated by the powerful), which is why there are strong demands for reform (e.g., expanding the Security Council to include rising powers like India)
The world is governed by a single all-powerful world government
Only the five permanent members matter in the world
solution: The chapter's overall message is that INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATIONS play a VITAL but LIMITED role in world politics. Above all, the UNITED NATIONS (established in 1945, succeeding the failed League of Nations) — with its main organs: the GENERAL ASSEMBLY (universal membership, one vote each, mostly non-binding resolutions), the SECURITY COUNCIL (primary responsibility for peace and security, with five VETO-wielding PERMANENT members and ten non-permanent members), the SECRETARIAT (headed by the Secretary-General), the INTERNATIONAL COURT of JUSTICE, and ECOSOC, plus SPECIALISED AGENCIES like the WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO, ILO, and FAO — together with the major economic institutions (the IMF, the WORLD BANK, and the WTO), help sovereign states to COOPERATE, MAINTAIN PEACE, RESOLVE DISPUTES peacefully, promote DEVELOPMENT and HUMAN RIGHTS, and tackle COMMON GLOBAL PROBLEMS. Alongside states, non-state actors like NGOs and MNCs also matter. However, these organisations have important LIMITATIONS: they DEPEND on the cooperation and will of their member states and CANNOT COMPEL great powers (especially given the Security Council VETO), and key bodies (the Security Council, and the Western-dominated IMF/World Bank) are widely seen as UNREPRESENTATIVE and DOMINATED by the powerful and outdated (reflecting 1945). This is why there are strong demands for REFORM — notably to EXPAND the Security Council to include RISING POWERS like INDIA and make it more representative and effective. So the overall message is option 2.

stem: The UN's peacekeeping forces are often called __________ because of the colour of the helmets/berets worn by the soldiers.
solution: The UN's PEACEKEEPING forces are often called the 'BLUE HELMETS' (or 'Blue Berets') because of the distinctive light-BLUE helmets and berets worn by the soldiers, who are contributed by member states but serve under the UN flag. These peacekeepers are deployed (with the consent of the parties) to help maintain ceasefires, monitor conflicts, and support peace in troubled regions. India has been one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping. So UN peacekeepers are called the 'Blue Helmets'. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), a landmark UN document, __________.
options: Set out fundamental human rights to be universally protected, serving as a common standard for all nations
solution: The UNIVERSAL DECLARATION of HUMAN RIGHTS (adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948) is a landmark document that SET OUT fundamental HUMAN RIGHTS and freedoms (civil, political, economic, social, and cultural) to be UNIVERSALLY protected for all human beings. It serves as a COMMON STANDARD of achievement for all nations and peoples, and it has profoundly influenced international human-rights law, national constitutions, and global norms. So the Universal Declaration set out universal human rights as a common standard. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The UN agency responsible for helping and protecting refugees is the __________.
solution: The UNHCR — the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (the UN Refugee Agency) — is the UN body responsible for HELPING and PROTECTING REFUGEES (and other displaced people) around the world. It provides shelter, aid, and legal protection to those forced to flee their homes by war, persecution, or disaster, and works toward durable solutions for them. So the UN refugee agency is the UNHCR. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: For India, active engagement with international organisations like the UN is important because __________.
options: It allows India to promote its interests and values, contribute to global issues (peacekeeping, development, climate), press for reform (like Security Council expansion), and enhance its global standing
India has no interest in the world
It forces India to give up its sovereignty
solution: For INDIA, active engagement with international organisations like the UN is important because it allows India to: PROMOTE its own INTERESTS and VALUES on the world stage; CONTRIBUTE to addressing global issues (e.g., through UN PEACEKEEPING — India is a leading troop contributor — and on DEVELOPMENT, CLIMATE, and disarmament); PRESS for REFORMS that would benefit developing countries and give India its due (notably, expansion of the Security Council to include India as a permanent member); and ENHANCE its GLOBAL STANDING and influence as a responsible major power. So engagement serves India's interests, its global contributions, its reform agenda, and its standing. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The WTO succeeded which earlier arrangement that had governed international trade since 1948?
options: The GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)
solution: The World Trade Organisation (WTO), established in 1995, SUCCEEDED the earlier arrangement known as the GATT — the GENERAL AGREEMENT on TARIFFS and TRADE — which had governed international trade since 1948. The GATT was a set of multilateral agreements aimed at reducing tariffs and trade barriers; the WTO built on and institutionalised this system into a permanent organisation with wider scope and a stronger dispute-settlement mechanism. So the WTO succeeded the GATT. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): Developing countries often push for reform of the IMF and World Bank. Reason (R): The voting power in these institutions is based on financial contributions, giving rich Western countries dominant control and leaving developing nations with little say. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that developing countries often PUSH for REFORM of the IMF and World Bank. And the reason is (R) that the VOTING POWER in these institutions is based on members' FINANCIAL CONTRIBUTIONS (quotas/shares), which gives the RICH WESTERN countries (especially the USA) DOMINANT control over decisions, while DEVELOPING nations — despite being the main borrowers and a large share of the world's population — have comparatively LITTLE SAY. This inequitable, wealth-weighted governance directly motivates the developing countries' demands for reform (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The overall importance of international organisations in an interconnected world is that they __________.
options: Provide essential mechanisms for managing global interdependence and collective problems (peace, trade, health, environment, development) that no single country can solve alone
Are irrelevant in a globalised world
Replace the need for any national governments
Only serve the interests of one country
solution: The overall importance of international organisations in today's deeply INTERCONNECTED (globalised) world is that they provide ESSENTIAL MECHANISMS for MANAGING global INTERDEPENDENCE and COLLECTIVE PROBLEMS — challenges such as maintaining PEACE and security, regulating TRADE, tackling pandemics and HEALTH crises, addressing the ENVIRONMENT and climate change, and promoting DEVELOPMENT — problems that NO SINGLE country can effectively solve ALONE and that require cooperation and coordination among nations. By providing forums, rules, and machinery for such cooperation, international organisations are indispensable to global governance. So they are essential for managing global interdependence and collective problems. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The UN was founded by the countries that were victorious in the Second World War, and its founding conference/charter was signed in __________.
solution: The United Nations was founded chiefly by the ALLIED countries victorious in the Second World War. Its founding CONFERENCE was held, and its CHARTER signed, at SAN FRANCISCO in 1945 (the UN Charter was signed in June 1945 and came into force in October 1945). So the UN Charter was signed at San Francisco in 1945. (Geneva was associated with the League of Nations; Yalta hosted a wartime Allied conference; Vienna hosted the 1815 Congress.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: A challenge for the future effectiveness of the UN and other international organisations is __________.
options: Adapting to a changing world (new powers, new threats like terrorism and climate change) and becoming more representative, democratic, and effective, while retaining the support of member states
solution: A key CHALLENGE for the future EFFECTIVENESS of the UN and other international organisations is ADAPTING to a rapidly CHANGING WORLD. This includes: accommodating NEW POWERS and shifting balances (e.g., reforming the Security Council to reflect today's realities); confronting NEW and transnational THREATS (such as terrorism, climate change, pandemics, cyber-threats, and economic crises) that require collective action; and becoming more REPRESENTATIVE, DEMOCRATIC, and EFFECTIVE and less paralysed — all WHILE retaining the essential SUPPORT and cooperation of member states (without which they cannot function). Meeting these challenges is vital to their continued relevance. So the challenge is adapting and reforming to remain representative and effective. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The number of non-permanent members of the UN Security Council is __________, elected for two-year terms.
solution: The UN Security Council has TEN non-permanent members, elected by the General Assembly for TWO-YEAR terms (with regional distribution). Together with the five permanent members (P5), this makes a TOTAL of 15 members. India has served several times as a non-permanent member. So there are ten non-permanent members. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the UN, is located at __________.
solution: The INTERNATIONAL COURT of JUSTICE (ICJ) — the principal JUDICIAL organ of the UN — is located at THE HAGUE in the Netherlands. It settles legal disputes submitted to it by states and gives advisory opinions on legal questions referred by UN organs. (The UN's main headquarters, by contrast, is in New York.) So the ICJ is at The Hague. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The headquarters of the United Nations is located in __________.
solution: The HEADQUARTERS of the United Nations is located in NEW YORK City (USA), where the General Assembly, Security Council, and Secretariat are based. (The UN also has major offices in Geneva, Vienna, and Nairobi, and the ICJ sits at The Hague.) So the UN's headquarters is in New York. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: India was a founding member of the United Nations and has contributed notably by __________.
options: Being one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping missions, and participating actively in UN development, human rights, and disarmament efforts
solution: India was a FOUNDING member of the United Nations (it joined in 1945, even before formal independence). India has contributed notably to the UN in many ways — most prominently by being ONE of the LARGEST CONTRIBUTORS of TROOPS to UN PEACEKEEPING missions around the world (Indian soldiers have served in numerous conflict zones under the UN flag), and by participating actively in UN efforts on DEVELOPMENT, HUMAN RIGHTS, DECOLONISATION, and DISARMAMENT. So India has contributed especially through peacekeeping and active participation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The organisation focused on labour rights and standards for workers worldwide is the __________.
solution: The INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANISATION (ILO) is the specialised agency focused on LABOUR — promoting workers' RIGHTS, decent working conditions, social protection, and fair labour STANDARDS worldwide. It is notable for its 'tripartite' structure, bringing together governments, employers, and workers' representatives. So the labour-focused body is the ILO. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The 'Bretton Woods' institutions, created in 1944 to manage the post-war international economy, are the __________.
solution: The 'BRETTON WOODS' institutions — named after the 1944 conference at Bretton Woods (USA) that created them to manage the post-war international economy — are the INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND (IMF) and the WORLD BANK. The IMF was set up to oversee the monetary/financial system and provide balance-of-payments support, and the World Bank to finance reconstruction and development. Together they form the core of the post-war international economic order. So the Bretton Woods institutions are the IMF and the World Bank. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The World Health Organisation (WHO) plays a crucial role, as seen in its efforts on __________.
options: Global public health — coordinating responses to diseases and pandemics, promoting health standards, and running immunisation and disease-eradication programmes
solution: The WORLD HEALTH ORGANISATION (WHO) plays a crucial role in GLOBAL PUBLIC HEALTH. It coordinates international responses to DISEASES and PANDEMICS (as seen during global health crises), sets and promotes health STANDARDS and guidelines, supports IMMUNISATION campaigns, and runs disease-CONTROL and ERADICATION programmes (for example, the eradication of smallpox). Its work is vital for protecting and improving health worldwide. So the WHO's crucial role is in global public health. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One argument AGAINST simply abolishing the veto or drastically changing the Security Council is that __________.
options: The great powers might lose interest in, or withdraw support from, the UN if their special status were removed — potentially weakening the organisation (as happened to the League of Nations)
The veto has no effect on anything
Small countries want the veto abolished for no reason
solution: One argument AGAINST simply abolishing the veto or radically overhauling the Security Council is a PRACTICAL/political one: the GREAT POWERS (the P5) might LOSE INTEREST in, or WITHDRAW their SUPPORT from, the UN if their special privileged STATUS (the veto) were removed. Since the UN depends heavily on the cooperation, resources, and participation of the major powers, alienating them could WEAKEN or even cripple the organisation — recalling how the LEAGUE of NATIONS failed partly because key powers did not join or support it. So the veto, though undemocratic, helps keep the great powers engaged. This is a real dilemma in UN reform. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The G-77 (Group of 77) at the UN is __________.
options: A coalition of developing countries that works to promote their collective economic interests and negotiating power in international forums
A group of the richest 77 corporations
solution: The G-77 (Group of 77) is a COALITION of DEVELOPING COUNTRIES at the United Nations (it began with 77 members and has since grown larger). It works to PROMOTE the collective ECONOMIC INTERESTS of the developing world and to enhance their joint NEGOTIATING POWER and voice in international forums and negotiations (on trade, development, finance, etc.). By banding together, developing countries can better press their common demands (such as those associated with the New International Economic Order) against the more powerful developed nations. So the G-77 is a coalition of developing countries. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The effectiveness of UN peacekeeping depends significantly on __________.
options: The consent and cooperation of the parties to a conflict, the mandate given by the Security Council, and the troops and funding contributed by member states
solution: The effectiveness of UN PEACEKEEPING depends significantly on several factors: the CONSENT and COOPERATION of the PARTIES to the conflict (peacekeepers are generally deployed with the agreement of the warring sides and to help keep an agreed peace, not to impose one by force); the MANDATE and authorisation given by the SECURITY COUNCIL (which defines what the mission can do); and the TROOPS, resources, and FUNDING CONTRIBUTED by member states (the UN has no army of its own and relies on voluntary contributions). Where these are lacking, peacekeeping struggles. So peacekeeping's effectiveness depends on consent, mandate, and member-state contributions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The UN has both successes and failures in maintaining peace. Reason (R): It can act effectively when the great powers agree, but is often paralysed when their interests clash and the veto is used. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the UN has had BOTH SUCCESSES and FAILURES in maintaining peace. And the reason is (R) that it can act EFFECTIVELY when the GREAT POWERS (the P5) AGREE (allowing the Security Council to authorise strong action), but it is often PARALYSED when their INTERESTS CLASH and one of them uses the VETO to block action. Thus the UN's peace record swings between success and failure largely depending on great-power agreement — which directly explains the mixed record (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches the organisation with its function?
options: WHO — health; WTO — trade; IMF — monetary stability/loans; World Bank — development lending; UNESCO — education/culture
WHO — trade; WTO — health; IMF — education; World Bank — nuclear energy
UNESCO — trade; IMF — refugees; WHO — labour; WTO — culture
All these organisations do the same thing
solution: The correct matching is: WHO (World Health Organisation) — HEALTH; WTO (World Trade Organisation) — TRADE; IMF (International Monetary Fund) — MONETARY STABILITY and balance-of-payments LOANS; WORLD BANK — long-term DEVELOPMENT LENDING; and UNESCO — EDUCATION, science, and CULTURE. Knowing which body handles which function is prelims-relevant. So option 1 gives the correct pairings.

stem: The relationship between national sovereignty and international organisations involves a tension because __________.
options: States want the benefits of cooperation but are reluctant to surrender their sovereignty/independence to international bodies, which limits how much power these organisations can have
States have no sovereignty at all
International organisations have unlimited power over states
There is no relationship between them
solution: The relationship between national SOVEREIGNTY and international organisations involves an inherent TENSION. On one hand, states WANT the BENEFITS of international COOPERATION (peace, trade, solutions to shared problems). On the other hand, they are RELUCTANT to SURRENDER their SOVEREIGNTY and INDEPENDENCE — their ultimate authority to decide their own affairs — to international bodies. This reluctance LIMITS how much power and authority international organisations can be given: states generally retain the final say and can resist or ignore decisions they dislike. This tension between the desire for cooperation and the guarding of sovereignty is central to understanding both the potential and the limits of international organisations. So the tension is between wanting cooperation and guarding sovereignty. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A balanced view of the UN concludes that __________.
options: Though imperfect and in need of reform, the UN remains indispensable — there is no better alternative for global cooperation, and the world is better off with it than without it
The UN should be abolished immediately
The UN is a flawless organisation needing no change
The UN has achieved nothing at all
solution: A BALANCED VIEW of the UN concludes that, though it is IMPERFECT — hampered by great-power dominance, the veto, unrepresentative structures, and various failures — and though it is genuinely in NEED of REFORM, the UN nevertheless remains INDISPENSABLE. There is no better ALTERNATIVE available for organising global cooperation, maintaining a forum for all nations, and addressing shared problems; and, on balance, the world is considerably BETTER OFF WITH the UN (with its peacekeeping, humanitarian, development, health, and norm-setting work) than it would be WITHOUT it. The sensible course is therefore to REFORM and strengthen the UN, not to abandon it. So the balanced conclusion is that the UN is imperfect but indispensable. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The key lesson about international organisations for a country like India is that India should __________.
options: Engage actively and constructively with them — using them to advance its interests and global goals, while pushing for reforms that make them fairer and more representative
Try to control them by force
solution: The key lesson for a country like INDIA is that it should ENGAGE ACTIVELY and CONSTRUCTIVELY with international organisations. India should USE these bodies to ADVANCE its national INTERESTS and its broader GLOBAL GOALS (peace, development, a fairer world order), CONTRIBUTE to them (as it does through peacekeeping and multilateral diplomacy), and simultaneously PUSH for REFORMS that make them FAIRER, more DEMOCRATIC, and more REPRESENTATIVE of today's world (such as expanding the Security Council to include India and other developing/rising powers). Active, reform-minded engagement — rather than boycott or indifference — best serves India's interests. So India should engage actively while pushing for reform. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, international organisations are best understood as __________.
options: Necessary and useful instruments of international cooperation and global governance — powerful in some respects but limited by the sovereignty and power of states, and in need of reform to serve a changing world
solution: In conclusion, international organisations are best understood as NECESSARY and USEFUL INSTRUMENTS of international COOPERATION and global GOVERNANCE. They are POWERFUL and consequential in some respects (setting rules, providing forums, running vast humanitarian, development, health, and peacekeeping operations, and shaping norms), yet they are fundamentally LIMITED by the SOVEREIGNTY and POWER of states — they cannot compel great powers and depend on members' cooperation. And, to remain effective and legitimate, they are in NEED of REFORM to serve a CHANGING WORLD (e.g., a more representative Security Council and fairer economic institutions). So they are indispensable but limited and reform-needing instruments of cooperation — not world governments, nor useless bodies. So option 1 is correct.
